title: Expanding Expressions

findings.finding: The opening review omits signed multiplication with a negative factor, although the introductory example directly requires negative-times-positive and negative-times-negative products.
findings.breakdown: In −x(2y−z), students must obtain both −2xy and +xz. A student who recalls distribution but misremembers the sign rule can produce −2xy−xz. The review's positive outside multipliers do not rehearse this decision.
findings.checked: Checked all nine review parts and the teaching preceding p4-example-demonstration. Neither sign combination with a negative outside factor is rehearsed. The distributive-law statement does not explain signed multiplication; subsequent guided practice does not supply an opening review.
findings.assumptions: Signed multiplication is prior knowledge from Computation with Integers. No calculator is assumed; the issue is choosing signs.

repair.proposal: Append to p3-q1-block: Calculate (j) (−3)×4; (k) (−3)×(−4); (l) (−1)×(−7). Answers: −12, 12, 7. Keep the complete review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: The opening review rehearses both sign combinations before the worked example.

findings.finding: Five whole practice tasks each appear twice without an explicit retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.breakdown: The identical pairs are p5-q1-a/j, p5-q1-k/t, p5-q2-a/j, p5-q2-k/t and p7-q5-a/b. Each later copy repeats the instruction, expression, values and required response.
findings.checked: Compared every targeted complete task. No targeted task has a diagram or additional given that distinguishes its copies. The surrounding variations do not state an instructional purpose for these exact repetitions. Tasks with equivalent answers but different expressions were not counted.
findings.assumptions: No additional teacher-directed purpose for the identical copies is specified.

repair.proposal: Keep each first copy. Replace p5-q1-j with 3(x+5), answer 3x+15; p5-q1-t with −6(3−x), answer −18+6x; p5-q2-j with x(x+5), answer x²+5x; p5-q2-t with −3x(3−x), answer −9x+3x²; and p7-q5-b with 3([blank]+4)=3x+12, answer x.

findings.doneWhen: Each unnecessary later copy has different numbers while retaining its original task structure, and its answer is updated.

findings.finding: Extend the existing sign variations by comparing expressions with the same expansion.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects the outside negative sign with the sign of every distributed product, using the existing expressions and numbers.
findings.checked: −3(−x−4)=3x+12, matching both p5-q1-a and p5-q1-b. Also, 3(−x−4)=−3(x+4)=−3x−12. These identities hold for every real x and require only distribution and comparison of expressions already available in this topic.
findings.assumptions: Offer as an optional follow-up after p5-q1-t.

repair.proposal: Add (u) Expand −3(−x−4). Answer: 3x+12. (v) Which expressions in parts (a)–(f) have the same expansion as part (u)? Answer: (a) and (b). (w) Explain why 3(−x−4) and −3(x+4) have the same expansion. Expected answer: both expand to −3x−12 because their distributed products are −3x and −12.

findings.doneWhen: The optional follow-up has separate parts and the stated expected answers.

findings.finding: Extend the existing pair with first factor x+2 into a four-question sequence varying only the second constant.
findings.breakdown: Keeping the first factor fixed exposes how changing the second constant changes both the linear coefficient and the constant term, including when the constant becomes negative.
findings.checked: The four expansions are correct for every real x. Existing parts c and d supply the first and third members. Parts a–f do not already contain a comparable three-to-five-question run with this feature held fixed. The unpatterned follow-up uses methods demonstrated in p18-guided-d.
findings.assumptions: Retain the existing area-model instruction and provide matching blank area grids for the added parts.

repair.proposal: Arrange this run together after p19-q1-b, reusing existing c and d rather than duplicating them: (x+2)(x+3), answer x²+5x+6; (x+2)(x+1), answer x²+3x+2; (x+2)(x−1), answer x²+x−2; (x+2)(x−3), answer x²−x−6. Add only this instruction: 'Predict how the answer will change before expanding each expression.' Immediately follow the run with (3x−1)(x+4), answer 3x²+11x−4. Retain existing e and f afterwards and relabel parts consecutively.

findings.doneWhen: The four expressions form one uninterrupted run, followed by the unpatterned expression, with existing tasks printed only once.

findings.finding: Use the existing paired square expansions to explore cancellation when their results are subtracted.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects p21-q1-g and p21-q1-h: their squared and constant terms cancel, leaving a linear expression that supports a numerical comparison.
findings.checked: Subtracting x²−6x+9 from x²+6x+9 gives 12x for every real x. Setting x=10 gives 13²−7²=120. Setting 12x=60 gives x=5. Expansion, subtraction of expressions and collecting like terms are available by this topic; the last part requires only elementary linear-equation solving.
findings.assumptions: Elementary linear-equation solving is prior knowledge, consistent with the separate Solve 2 step equations booklet.

repair.proposal: After p21-q1-r, add optional parts: (s) Use your expansions in parts (g) and (h) to simplify (x+3)²−(x−3)². Answer: 12x. (t) How much larger is 13² than 7²? Answer: 120. (u) Find x when (x+3)² is 60 greater than (x−3)². Answer: x=5.

findings.doneWhen: The optional follow-up is presented as three separate parts with the stated expected answers.
